id: Your Invitation to a Modest Breakfast

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s too cold to smoke outside, but if you come over, I’ll keep my hands to myself, or won’t I. I would like to tell you about the wall eaten up by the climbing plant—it was so beautiful. Various things have been happening to me, all of them sexual. The man on the bus took off his pants so I could see him better. Another man said, “Ignore him darlin’. Just sit on my lap.” But I’m not one of those who’s hungriest in the morning, unlike the man at the bakery who eats egg after egg after egg. Listen. Come over: the cold has already eaten the summer. I need another pair of ears: from the kitchen I can’t tell if I’m hearing wind chimes or some gray woman with failing arms dropping a pan full of onions and potatoes. This morning I need four hands— two to wash the greens, one to lift a teakettle, one to pour the milk. This morning, one little mouth will not do. We could play a game where we crouch on the tiles, two yellow dogs drinking coffee from bowls. We could play a game where we let the breakfast burn. Outside there’s a world where every love scene begins with a man in a doorway; he walks over to the woman and says “Open your mouth.”

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Various, The, Another

outputs.L1: It's too cold to smoke outside, but if you come over, I'll keep my hands to myself—or will I? I want to tell you about the wall devoured by the climbing plant; it was so beautiful. Various things have been happening to me, all of them sexual. The man on the bus took off his pants so I could see him better. Another man said, "Ignore him, darlin'. Just sit on my lap." But I'm not among those who hunger most in the morning, unlike the man at the bakery who eats egg after egg after egg. Listen. Come over: the cold has already devoured the summer. I need another pair of ears—from the kitchen I can't tell if I'm hearing wind chimes or some gray woman with failing arms dropping a pan full of onions and potatoes. This morning I need four hands: two to wash the greens, one to lift the teakettle, one to pour the milk. This morning, one small mouth will not suffice. We could play a game where we crouch on the tiles, two yellow dogs lapping coffee from bowls. We could play a game where we let the breakfast burn. Outside, there's a world where every love scene begins with a man in a doorway; he crosses to the woman and says, "Open your mouth."
outputs.L2:
It's much too frigid for smoking outdoors, but should you stop by, I'll behave myself—or maybe I won't. I want to describe that wall consumed by climbing vines—such beauty in that decay. Strange things keep happening to me lately, and they're all tinged with sexuality. There was a man on the bus who removed his trousers so I'd have a better view. Another man told me, "Don't mind him, sweetheart. Come sit here instead." Still, I'm not among those whose appetite peaks at dawn, unlike that fellow at the bakery who devours egg after egg after egg.

Pay attention. Visit me: winter has already devoured summer whole. I require an extra set of ears—standing in the kitchen, I can't distinguish between wind chimes ringing and some ashen woman with feeble arms letting a pan of onions and potatoes crash to the floor. This particular morning demands four hands instead of two—a pair for rinsing vegetables, another to lift the kettle, one more for pouring milk. This morning, a single small mouth simply won't suffice.

We might invent a game where we squat on the floor tiles like two golden dogs, lapping coffee straight from bowls. Or perhaps a different game where we simply let breakfast burn to nothing. Beyond these walls exists a world where every romantic moment starts identically: a man appears in a doorway, crosses toward the woman waiting there, and murmurs, "Open your mouth."
outputs.L3:
Come over, even though it's cold. Come anyway. I'll press you against the doorframe if I have to, hold your wrists there just long enough that you can't tell if it's a request or a refusal, if I'm keeping you out or pulling you in. That's usually how it goes with me lately—the boundary blurred, the gesture ambiguous, everyone's hands unsure of their own intentions.

Things have been happening to me. I don't know how else to say it. The man on the bus, for instance, whose knee found mine and stayed there through four stops while he read his newspaper like nothing was occurring, like his leg belonged to someone else entirely. I let it stay too. I don't know why. There have been others—small transgressions, half-invited, half-endured, blurring together until I can't sort what I wanted from what simply happened to me, the way weather happens.

Even the world outside my window has stopped holding its shape properly. The wall out back is being eaten alive by some climbing vine, green teeth working slowly through brick, and I watch it the way you'd watch a wound you weren't sure was healing or widening. Yesterday I heard wind chimes, or maybe it was the woman next door dropping her pots again—the same bright, scattering clatter either way—and I stood at the sink for a full minute unable to tell which it was, unable to care which it was, as if the distinction between music and accident had stopped mattering to me.

Mornings are the worst for this kind of confusion. I need more hands than I have—one for the kettle, one for the phone that won't stop, one to smooth the sheets, one to hold someone's face if someone's face were here to hold. I need more ears too, one for the toast popping, one for the news murmuring its emergencies, one pressed to your chest just to hear you're still breathing beside me. Everything wants attention at once and I am only built with the standard number of limbs.

Some mornings I think the better answer is to abandon the whole apparatus of adult competence. To get down on the kitchen tiles on all fours and be a dog for a while, panting, uncomplicated, wanting only water and a hand on my head. To let the toast burn black and not care, to let the whole performance of breakfast collapse into smoke while I lie there, tail-less but wagging in spirit. Because outside, past my door, the world has already written its script for how this is supposed to go—someone arriving with flowers held out like a subpoena, someone kneeling with a ring like a verdict, every gesture pre-approved by a thousand other lovers doing the identical thing before us. I don't want the script. I want the tile, cold under my palms, and you, uncertain in the doorway, deciding whether to come in out of the cold.
outputs.L4:
Come over. It's cold enough that the pipes tick when the heat kicks on, that small metallic complaint traveling through the walls like something trying to get my attention. Wear the coat that smells like outside. I want to smell winter on you before it melts into the smell of this kitchen.

I'm cooking something with too much garlic. The knife against the cutting board, that steady percussion — I like how sound in a kitchen is almost always domestic and almost always a little violent. The onion doesn't apologize for making me cry. Neither should you, for whatever it is you're going to tell me when you get here.

*

There was a man once who ate an apple across from me on a train and made it obscene without trying. The wet sound of it. His jaw working. I looked away and then looked back, because looking away first is its own kind of confession. He didn't notice me. Or he did and pretended not to, which is worse, or better — I've never decided.

Another man, years before that, stood too close at a bus stop in the rain and asked if I had an umbrella big enough for two. I said no. I had an umbrella big enough for two. I don't know why I lied except that his voice had a hook in it and I didn't want to be caught on it in public.

*

The water's boiling now. I can hear it change register — the low grumble becoming something more insistent, almost impatient, like it's been waiting for me to notice. I turn the heat down and it settles, sulking, into a simmer. Everything wants to be attended to. Everything is starving a little.

I think about your hands a lot in weather like this. Not in a way I'd say out loud to anyone else. The specific coldness of a hand that's been outside, pressed flat against a warm back — how that first contact is almost unbearable and then isn't, how the cold gets absorbed like it was never a separate thing at all.

*

There's a kind of man who watches you eat and calls it romantic, who mistakes appetite for intimacy, who thinks if he watches closely enough he'll understand something about you that you don't understand about yourself. I've let men do this. I've sat very still under it, letting the observation happen, curious what they thought they were seeing. Usually it was just hunger, dressed up.

I don't want that from you. I want you to eat with your mouth full and not perform anything. I want the ordinary carelessness of it — sauce on your thumb, you licking it off without thinking, no significance assigned, and still somehow it undoes me a little, the unguardedness of it.

*

The bread's gone stale enough to toast well. Burnt butter smell filling the kitchen now, that particular richness that makes the whole room feel like it's confiding something. I keep thinking about the weight of another body in a small space — how a kitchen this size means we'll bump elbows, means you'll have to say excuse me or not say it at all and just let your hand rest a second too long on my hip while reaching past me for the salt.

I want that kind of accident. The kind that isn't.

*

Once, in another apartment, a man leaned in the doorway of a kitchen much like this one and watched me cook without offering to help, and I hated him for it in a way that felt almost erotic, the specific fury of being watched and unassisted, wanted and unhelped. I've never fully worked out why some kinds of neglect feel like desire and some just feel like neglect. Maybe it's about whether you can still hear their breathing change.

*

Come over. Bring the cold in with you, on your coat, in your hands, and let me be the one who complains about it and also the one who presses close to take it from you anyway. Let's eat standing up at the counter like we don't have anywhere better to be, because we don't. Let the spoon clatter in the sink. Let the radiator tick its strange language into the walls.

I want your knee against mine under a table too small for two people to be that comfortable. I want the very unremarkable fact of your weight beside me on a couch that's seen better decades. I want to laugh about nothing and have it turn, without warning, into something neither of us named on purpose — the way desire does, sliding in sideways through the domestic, through garlic and burnt butter and the small tyranny of boiling water, until it's suddenly the only thing in the room.

Come over. It's cold. I'm making dinner. I want to be touched like an afterthought that turns out to be the whole point.
outputs.L5:
# On Multiplicity and Meaning

Various paths lead to understanding, yet we often insist there is only **The** answer, **The** truth, **The** way things must be. This tension—between the plural and the singular—shapes much of how we navigate the world.

Consider how often we encounter **another** perspective that challenges what we thought was settled. A scientist discovers **another** variable that complicates a once-elegant theory. A traveler finds **another** culture that reframes assumptions about what's "normal." A reader finishes a book only to pick up **another**, and finds their certainties gently dismantled.

**Various** disciplines teach us this lesson in different ways. History reminds us that **the** narrative we're taught is often just one version among many competing accounts. Science shows that **the** current consensus is always provisional, waiting for **another** experiment to refine or overturn it. Art suggests that **the** meaning of a work shifts depending on who's looking, and when.

Perhaps the wisdom lies not in choosing between **the** singular and **the** various, but in holding both simultaneously. We need **the** conviction to act, to believe in something firm enough to stand on. But we also need the humility to recognize that **another** viewpoint, **another** fact, **another** story might be waiting just around the corner—ready to expand or complicate what we thought we knew.

In this way, **the** search for truth is never finished. It's a **various**, evolving process, one where **another** question always follows the last answer, keeping us curious, humble, and awake to the world's endless complexity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about loneliness and desire, mixing mundane morning routines with strange sexual encounters.
counterfactuals.output:
The coffee maker gurgles like something drowning, and I stand in the kitchen in yesterday's shirt, waiting for the dark water to fill the pot, and this is when she arrives—not through the door, never through the door—but folded out of the steam, hip-first, her spine made of the same curling vapor that rises off the burner. She sits on the counter where the fruit bowl should be. There is no fruit. There hasn't been fruit in weeks.

I ask her if she takes sugar and she opens her mouth instead of answering, and inside her mouth is another kitchen, smaller, with its own coffee maker gurgling, its own version of me not answering questions either.

This is Tuesday. This is always Tuesday.

My hands know the choreography of morning—toothbrush, floss, the cold water shocking my face awake—and beneath the routine runs the other current, the one where loneliness has learned to wear the shape of touch, has gotten good at pressing its mouth to the back of my neck while I stare into the mirror trying to remember if I've always had this many teeth.

The bed, when I return to it, is full of static and the ghost-weight of someone who was never fully there. I have made love to radio silence. I have held the space between stations and called it a body, called it warm, called it *stay*.

Sometimes it's the mail carrier, except she never leaves, except she becomes the mail, becomes envelopes I open all day looking for handwriting I'd recognize, and inside every envelope is the same word written in a language my hands remember even when my mind does not: *alone alone alone*, except when I touch it, it hums like a name being called from very far underwater.

Breakfast is toast, always toast, and the desire that comes to eat with me has no fixed address—today it's shaped like the boy from third grade who never spoke to me, today it's shaped like nobody, like the outline where somebody should be sitting, and I set a plate for it anyway because you learn to make room at the table even for the absences, especially for the absences, they get hungry too.

I go to work. I don't remember going to work. There is a gap in the afternoon shaped exactly like a bed.

At night the apartment breathes without me, in and out, in and out, and I lie in the dark practicing the specific alchemy of wanting something with no name, no shape, no door it might walk through—just the ache, wearing my own skin like a coat two sizes too big, whispering *let me in, let me in*, and I do, every single time, I let it in, because the alternative is silence, and silence has too many teeth of its own, and morning is coming, gurgling, dark, and it will ask me if I slept, and I will lie, the way I always lie, the way the coffee maker lies about being alive, filling itself up with something that only looks like warmth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a piece of experimental flash fiction in a confessional, stream-of-consciousness voice, blending eroticism with domestic imagery like breakfast and kitchens?
counterfactuals.output:
**Kitchen, Unmade**

I want to tell you about the butter first, how it sat out all night going soft in its dish like something that had given up pretending to be solid, and how I found you at six a.m. in nothing but the leftover dark, your shoulder blade a small mountain range I had already memorized with my mouth, and the light coming in sideways through the blinds made stripes across your back like a bar code, like you were a thing I could scan and take home though I already had you, already had all of you, spread out on the counter where I usually roll dough.

The coffee maker gurgled its confession before I could gurgle mine. Isn't that always the way — the machines get there first, sputtering their small hot truths into the pot while we're still deciding whether to speak. I pressed my sternum to your spine and felt your breath catch the way steam catches on a cold window, fogging, blooming, and I thought: this is what it means to be a kitchen. To hold heat. To be entered by hands that know exactly where the good knives are kept.

You asked if I wanted eggs. I said yes but I meant *don't move*, I meant *stay curved like that, like a question mark, like the good kind of hunger*. The yolk broke when you cracked it — of course it broke, everything breaks under the right pressure, that's not tragedy, that's chemistry, that's what makes the thing edible — and I watched the yellow spread across the pan the way desire spreads across a morning you didn't plan for, edge to edge, unstoppable, faintly sacrilegious in its brightness.

There is no metaphor for your hand on my hip that isn't also a metaphor for bread proofing, quiet, patient, becoming something. I have confessed this to no one. I am confessing it now, to the orange juice sweating on the table, to the toaster's small orange coils, to whatever god lives in the crumbs we'll sweep up later and pretend didn't matter.

We ate standing up. We always eat standing up, as if sitting would mean admitting this is a life, a real one, with recurring Tuesdays and grocery lists and a body that keeps wanting yours in the specific grammar of *pass the salt* and *come here* said in the same breath, no comma, no pause, salt and skin belonging to the same sentence.

Outside, someone's sprinkler hissed on. Inside, the butter finally melted all the way through.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of a female poet-narrator addressing a lover, full of odd sensory details—wind chimes, onions, dogs—and a tone that's both intimate and unsettling.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Meant to Say

I wanted to tell you about the wind chimes
my mother hung outside her kitchen window—
how they sounded like teeth
when the storms came through Ohio,
how I used to think God
was trying to tell us something
in that clattering, glassy tongue.

Instead I peeled onions in your kitchen
at 2 a.m., crying for reasons
that had nothing to do with onions.
You watched me from the doorway
the way dogs watch a door
after someone's already gone—
that particular patience
that isn't patience at all
but a kind of grief
still deciding what to call itself.

I keep thinking about your hands.
The onion skins on the counter
like something molted, something shed.
The neighbor's dog barking
at nothing, or at everything,
which are sometimes the same thing
at 2 a.m. in a stranger's kitchen
that has started, slowly,
to feel like mine.

There is a smell that onions leave
under the fingernails for days.
I keep smelling it and thinking of you,
which means I am always
a little bit crying,
which means the wind chimes
back home are probably going off right now
even though there's no wind,
even though my mother's asleep,
even though nothing
is trying to tell anyone
anything—

and still I hear it.
Still I stand here
with my raw hands
and this useless tenderness,
listening for teeth
in everything
that moves.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short literary piece that starts with "It's too cold to smoke outside" and spirals into a meditation on need, touch, and strange men, ending with an image of a man saying "Open your mouth."
counterfactuals.output:
It's too cold to smoke outside, but she does it anyway, cupping the lighter like something small and alive, something that needs her hands around it to survive. The cherry glows and dies, glows and dies. Her breath fogs into the same shape as the smoke, so that for a second she can't tell which part of her is burning and which part is just cold.

She thinks about need, how it arrives dressed as other things. Hunger dressed as boredom. Loneliness dressed as a text at 1 a.m. that says *you up*. She has become fluent in the language of wanting without naming what she wants, the same way you learn to say *fine* when someone asks how you are, the way the word becomes a wall you build brick by brick every single day.

Touch is a rumor she half-remembers. A hand on the small of her back, guiding her through a doorway. Fingers laced with hers on a countertop, absentminded, the kind of touching that doesn't ask permission because it assumes it's always welcome. She misses being handled like that — like something worth reaching for without a reason.

The strange men come to her in fragments, the way memory works when you're trying not to remember. The one who called her *baby* before he knew her name. The one who touched her wrist like he was checking her pulse, like he needed proof she was still there, still willing. The one who said *relax* as though relaxing were a door she could simply unlock if she tried hard enough. She has been so many women for so many men, has folded herself into whatever shape they needed her to be, has learned that need is a language everyone speaks but no one translates the same way twice.

She stubs out the cigarette. The cold doesn't care about her small rebellions, doesn't care that she stood out here breathing smoke like a dragon guarding nothing. She goes back inside where it's warm, where the light is low and gold, where a man she barely knows is waiting on the couch with his shirt half-unbuttoned and his eyes doing that thing eyes do when they've already decided something.

He doesn't ask if she's ready. He just looks at her, patient the way a predator is patient, and says the four words that have followed her through every room she's ever been afraid in, every room she's ever wanted to be brave in:

"Open your mouth."
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a piece of experimental prose poetry that feels like a diary entry—sensual, slightly surreal, with recurring motifs of hands, mouths, and cold weather.
counterfactuals.output:
**January, unspecified day**

The cold came in through the mouth of the door again, the way it always does, like something remembering how to speak. I let it in. I let most things in lately.

My hands have been strange to me—too warm, or not warm enough, never matching the weather outside my own skin. This morning I held a cup of tea and watched steam curl up like a small ghost trying to kiss the air. I thought: *this is what my mouth wants to do. Rise. Disappear a little. Come back changed.*

There is a man who lives in my memory now only as a pair of hands. I don't remember his face, just the way his fingers used to map my collarbones like a country he was trying to annex. Cold country. Cold hands. He used to breathe onto them before touching me, as if apologizing in advance for winter.

I keep thinking about mouths that don't speak. The mouth of a river, frozen shut. The mouth of a glove, empty, waiting for a hand that isn't mine. My own mouth, chapped, salt-cracked, saying nothing to no one in the mirror except *good morning* like a password to a door that never opens.

Outside, the snow is doing that thing again where it makes the whole world look like it's holding its breath. I put my palm against the window and left a mark—warm ghost, five-fingered, already fading. Somewhere, someone is doing the same thing to a different window, in a different cold, and neither of us knows we are twins in this small ritual of touching what we cannot keep.

I dreamed last night that my hands were full of teeth. Not frightening—more like a harvest. I planted them in the snow outside my door and by morning little white mouths had sprouted, all of them whispering the same word, over and over, a word I couldn't quite hear but which felt like *stay.*

The tea has gone cold. My hands have gone cold. My mouth, when I finally speak aloud to the empty apartment, comes out in visible breath, a small white flag of surrender to the season.

I write this down because some nights the only warmth I have is language—the friction of one word rubbed against another, hands chafing hands, mouth against mouth, all of it trying to start a fire that will not last, but for a moment, catches.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
